full_text:
The rich wife of a nobleman fell mortally ill. Calling her only daughter, sweet and pious, to her bedside, she whispered:
'Dear child, remain pious and good, and the dear God will always protect thee, and I will look down from heaven and be near thee.'
With these words, she closed her eyes. Every day the maiden went to her mother's grave beneath the weeping willow, weeping and remaining pious.

When winter passed, the nobleman took another wife, who brought two daughters with beautiful, fair faces but black, cruel hearts.
They took away the maiden’s fine dresses, clothed her in an old grey smock and wooden shoes, and drove her into the kitchen:
'Look at the proud princess, how she must work! If thou wilt eat bread, thou must earn it!'
From morning until dusk she carried water, kindled fires, cooked, and washed. At night, having no bed, she lay down in the ashes beside the hearth, wherefore they called her Aschenputtel.

One day, the father was going to the fair; he asked his stepdaughters what he should bring them:
'Beautiful dresses,' said the first.
'Pearls and diamonds,' said the second.
'And thou, Aschenputtel?' asked the father.
'Father, break off the first twig that brushes against your hat on the way home, and bring it to me.'

He brought the stepdaughters their jewels, and to Aschenputtel he gave a hazel twig.
She took the branch, planted it upon her mother's grave, and wept so bitterly that her tears watered the twig. It grew into a magnificent hazel tree. Three times a day Aschenputtel went beneath its boughs, and whenever she prayed, a white dove perched in the branches and granted whatever she wished.

The King proclaimed a three-day festival, that his son might choose a bride.
When the stepdaughters prepared to depart, Aschenputtel begged to go.
The stepmother threw a dish of lentils into the kitchen ashes: 'If thou canst pick these clean in two hours, thou shalt go!'
Aschenputtel went to the garden door and called:
'You gentle doves, you turtle-doves, all you birds beneath the sky,
Come and help me pick:
The good into the pot,
The bad into your crop!'

Flocks of white doves flew through the window, pecked with their beaks, and completed the task in half an hour.
Yet the stepmother laughed cruelly: 'Thou hast no clothes and canst not dance; thou wouldst only bring us shame!' and departed.

Left alone, Aschenputtel ran to the hazel tree and called:
'Rustle and shake, dear little tree,
Throw gold and silver over me!'

The white dove tossed down a gown woven of gold and silver silk, with slippers embroidered with silk and silver.
At the ball, the Prince took her hand and danced only with her. When evening fell, she slipped away into the pigeon-house and returned home, laying her finery beneath the tree.

On the second evening, the bird gave her an even more splendid dress; on the third evening, a gown radiant as the morning sun, with slippers of pure gold!
To capture her, the Prince had coated the palace staircase with pitch. As Aschenputtel fled, her left golden slipper stuck fast to the stair!

The Prince rode across the kingdom with the golden slipper:
'No other shall be my bride than she whose foot fits this golden shoe!'
The two stepsisters tried to force their feet into the shoe in their bedchambers, but their heels were far too large.
The Prince asked: 'Hast thou no other daughter?'
The father answered: 'Only a little stunted kitchen-drudge, child of my late wife.'

Aschenputtel washed her face and hands, came into the hall, and sat upon a stool.
She pulled her foot out of her heavy wooden shoe and stepped into the golden slipper: it fit her foot like a glove!
When she looked up, the Prince recognized the beautiful maiden who had danced with him:
'This is the true bride!'

The white dove fluttered down from the hazel tree, perching upon Aschenputtel's shoulder, cooing of truth and justice.
Aschenputtel rode beside the Prince to the royal castle, celebrated as Queen, proving that quiet piety and steadfast patience outlast the deepest winter.
moral: A pure heart grounded in ancestral love and honesty receives divine protection, while deception exposes its own folly.
